narrative.text: The acknowledgements of the consolidated HIV strategic information guidelines, naming WHO staff, external reviewers and contributing organizations. It also notes funding from the US government through USAID and CDC.
A list of abbreviations and acronyms used in the HIV strategic information guidelines.

A glossary of terms used in the HIV strategic information guidelines, from active TB disease and advanced HIV disease through aggregate data to key and vulnerable populations. It defines clinical, programme and data system concepts relevant to person-centred HIV monitoring. Definitions are generally given for both clinical and data-management purposes.

The executive summary of the consolidated HIV strategic information guidelines notes that despite abundant data, new infections remain above targets and retention and late diagnosis are problems. It explains that the guidelines focus on individual-level routine data to strengthen person-centred services and linkage to prevention and treatment. It also notes the inclusion of data on STIs, TB, viral hepatitis and cervical cancer in HIV data systems.

Summarizes the guidelines' recommendations by chapter, starting with new recommendations on collecting individual-level HIV prevention data to measure coverage and impact. Further recommendations cover testing, treatment, data systems and use of digital tools. It closes by stressing confidentiality and security of personal data, given elevated risks for key populations.

A summary table of priority indicators from WHO's 2022 consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information, giving each indicator's reference number, short name and definition, with new and updated indicators flagged. It spans HIV prevention (condoms, PrEP, PEP, needle–syringe programmes and more), testing, treatment and viral load, vertical transmission, and differentiated service delivery. It also covers TB–HIV, related infections such as cervical cancer, incidence and mortality, and ends with indicators on avoidance of health care due to stigma and discrimination.

The contents listing for Chapter 1, the introduction, covering background, evolving data needs, individual-level data, integration of related infections, key populations, new features, objectives, development process and intended audiences.

Describes progress in the HIV response, with about 28 million of 38 million people living with HIV on treatment in 2021, and new challenges such as loss to follow-up and slow declines in new infections. It argues that routine data systems must evolve to identify gaps faster, alongside surveys, studies and models, while keeping the people whose data are gathered safe and their data secure.

Contrasts aggregate facility data with individual-level data, explaining that person-level records linked by unique identifiers improve continuity of care, reduce duplicate counts and allow more accurate automated reporting. It describes how paper-based and electronic reporting may run in parallel while systems mature and be combined at subnational or national level. It stresses checking completeness and quality and the principle of collecting data once and using it many times.

Notes the large global burden of STIs, HPV, herpes and hepatitis B and C among people with HIV, and the overlap in transmission routes and services. It explains that the guidelines integrate these infections, along with TB and cervical cancer, into person-centred HIV monitoring through suggested minimum datasets and indicators.

Identifies five key populations disproportionately affected by HIV, viral hepatitis and STIs and the social, legal and structural barriers they face. It discusses the risks of recording key population status in routine data and advises against collecting such information where it could harm individuals or deter them from services.

Explains that HIV strategic information should fit within the wider health information system, illustrated by an integrated data architecture figure. It notes that routine data cover only people reached by services and should be triangulated with surveys, models and studies, and highlights community-based services and community-led monitoring.

Explains that the consolidated guidelines bring together data elements, indicators and data-system guidance across all HIV services, replacing two earlier WHO strategic information guidelines from 2017 and 2020. It describes implementation gaps in patient monitoring and case surveillance and the aim of linking individual-level and aggregate data under the collect-once-use-many principle. A box lists new areas, including the first minimum datasets for HIV prevention, STIs, viral hepatitis and cervical cancer.

Notes that while the guidelines focus on person-centred data, many settings lack mature integrated systems, so priority indicators can still be calculated with existing reporting. It explains how data from digital and paper systems can be combined during transition, with limits on deduplication, and the role of the guidance in common understanding among managers and developers.

Sets out the goal of helping countries generate person-centred data from routine health information systems and use it across the HIV cascade. It lists objectives, such as greater use of individual-level data linked by unique identifiers, and guiding principles including privacy, security, ethics, equity and governance.

Describes how WHO developed the guidelines through review of existing guidance, expert consultation, a Core Advisory Group and technical working groups for each programme area. It notes that external contributors completed declarations of interests.
Outlines the six technical chapters of the guidelines, the indicator metadata in Chapter 8, and web annexes containing the full minimum dataset and additional indicators and tools.
Identifies the intended users of the guidelines, chiefly national and subnational HIV programme managers, surveillance officers and partners, as well as NGOs, private providers and academics.
The reference list for the introduction chapter, citing UNAIDS global AIDS updates, population survey and incidence studies, and WHO guidance on strategic information and digital health.

The contents listing for Chapter 2 on person-centred HIV prevention monitoring, covering prevention epidemiology, individual-level prevention data, confidentiality and unique identifiers, minimum datasets, data use and indicators.

Sets out new key recommendations for HIV prevention monitoring: collecting a minimum individual-level dataset, using it to measure people reached and prevention impact, and recording clinical and behavioural risk factors to target services. It stresses safeguarding confidentiality when linking prevention data to other clinical datasets.

Describes slow declines in HIV incidence, with 1.5 million new infections in 2020, and the rising share among key populations and their partners. It notes that criminalization, stigma and discrimination create barriers that must be addressed for equitable access to prevention.

Explains why HIV prevention outcomes are hard to measure, since people start and stop prevention as needs change, and why multiple data sources are needed. The guidelines focus on routine programmatic data, which can also identify people at elevated risk and track whether interventions are received and used.

Advocates a person-centred, context-specific approach to HIV prevention delivered through varied settings, including community-led services, in line with the Global AIDS Strategy. It lists evidence-based biomedical and health-sector prevention interventions, from ART and PrEP to needle–syringe programmes and male circumcision, and notes that counselling alone has not shown an effect on incidence. It points to tools for setting prevention targets for key populations.

Notes that individual-level data have been central to HIV treatment cascades but little used for prevention, and lists prevention outcomes worth monitoring. It sets out the prerequisites for such data, including confidentiality, standardized tools and a minimum dataset.

Explains why confidentiality of individual-level data matters for key populations and adolescents whose behaviours may be criminalized, listing harms such as law enforcement use and underreporting of risk. It discusses the use of unique identification codes to link records while protecting anonymity, with further guidance in Chapter 6.

Discusses how intersecting factors such as age, gender and criminalization shape HIV risk and access to prevention, and how individual risk changes over time. It suggests building a process into health information systems to identify people most likely to benefit from prevention services.

Describes how client–provider conversations, held with privacy and often with peer support, help identify an individual's HIV prevention needs, and stresses offering prevention to anyone who asks without requiring explanation. It covers the use of prevention prioritization or risk assessment tools when people underestimate their risk, especially adolescents. It advises reassessing need regularly and gives example screening questions to adapt locally.

Explains in WHO's consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information how health data systems can capture HIV prevention need, through prioritization questions recorded during services and through records showing an individual has received services for key populations or other at-risk groups. It warns that people may not answer behavioural questions, so recorded need may be underestimated. It notes that trans and gender diverse people can be identified from data on sex assigned at birth and current gender identity.

Lists the many entry points where individual-level HIV prevention data can be recorded, such as HIV testing, STI, PrEP and PEP services, harm reduction, gender-based violence, family planning, antenatal care and youth programmes.

Describes registration in HIV prevention data systems, recommending an anonymous unique identifier rather than personal details, with contact information recorded only with informed consent and strong confidentiality safeguards. It lists the registration data to collect and suggests recording both current gender and sex assigned at birth where appropriate.

Recommends collecting a minimum set of individual-level data for each HIV prevention intervention, using event dates to show what happened and when, on paper or electronic tools. A table sets out the minimum dataset for interventions such as HIV testing, condoms, PrEP, needle–syringe programmes, opioid agonist maintenance treatment and voluntary medical male circumcision.

Describes how providers can use individual prevention records and automated alerts to follow up people who miss appointments or services, with reminders sent only with consent. It stresses protecting privacy when contacting people and referring them to other needed services such as STI or hepatitis care.

Explains how site-level aggregation of individual data can help monitor service use, outcomes, stock levels, follow-up and referrals, with automatic reporting through tools such as DHIS2 and dashboards.

Explains that indicators derived from routine individual-level data can reveal trends and programme gaps that once needed surveys, such as ongoing risk, prevention choices and whether people stay HIV-negative. It describes tracking unique individuals and commodity volumes and cohort-style analysis, and notes the importance of monitoring community-led services against Global AIDS Strategy targets.

Explains why HIV prevention cascades are harder to build than treatment cascades, since interventions are delivered in varied ways, risk changes over time, outcomes are non-linear and commodities come from many sources. It points to existing frameworks, including a PAHO approach for key populations, and advises reading prevention cascades alongside testing and treatment cascades.

Introduces the priority indicators for HIV prevention, drawing on individual-level programme data, aggregate data and surveys, with disaggregation by key population and other factors. A table defines each indicator with numerators and denominators, covering condom distribution and use, PrEP recipients, coverage and volume, and other prevention services. It ends with indicators on retesting among people at elevated risk who previously tested negative.

The reference list for the HIV prevention chapter of the strategic information guidelines, citing UN political declarations, UNAIDS strategies and data, WHO guidance and studies on prevention and community-led responses.

The table of contents for Chapter 3 on person-centred HIV patient monitoring for testing, early diagnosis and treatment, listing sections on HIV testing and linkage, ART initiation, retention and viral suppression, data quality and use, and country adaptation and digital transition.

Lists the chapter's key recommendations on HIV patient monitoring, marked as new or updated, including using routine testing data to reach undiagnosed people and support early diagnosis. They also cover using person-centred data to detect treatment interruption and support re-engagement, standardized digital tools, and monitoring differentiated service delivery and its outcomes.

Defines HIV patient monitoring as routinely gathering, analysing and using data about people with HIV across services and over time, mainly to guide clinical care and ensure continuity of testing and treatment. It lists further uses of the data, such as tracking epidemic trends, measuring programme performance and informing drug stock management to reduce wastage and stock-outs.

Describes how investments in digital health information systems, electronic medical records and unique identifiers have strengthened person-centred monitoring and led to a prioritized minimum dataset. It explains that the chapter updates WHO's 2017 patient monitoring guidance to cover the full care cascade and support differentiated service delivery. It also notes the expansion from 40 to 80 priority indicators, of which 36 come from patient monitoring and 25 are core, plus optional additional indicators for countries with stronger systems.

Explains that the updated guidance supports monitoring people as they move between facilities, recommending facility-held patient cards, ART registers or electronic records with data flowing in from community services, as well as new tools for differentiated service delivery. It describes the intended audiences and notes that pharmacy services and non-HIV TB and maternal and child health data elements are outside its scope.

A box summarizing new WHO HIV testing recommendations relevant to patient monitoring, including testing all pregnant women for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, dual HIV/syphilis rapid tests in antenatal care and differing approaches for high- and low-burden settings. It also covers self-testing, index and network-based testing and the need to update tools and records to track linkage between facilities and community services.

Explains that understanding people's HIV testing history and results guides their care and that monitoring should cover all prevention, testing and treatment service points. It outlines the purposes of testing data, such as optimizing case finding and linkage to ART and prevention, and presents a table of six priority HIV testing indicators. It ends with guidance on which partners and family members of index clients should be offered testing.

Notes that as more people living with HIV know their status, test positivity falls and reaching undiagnosed people becomes harder, making analysis of routine testing data essential. It explains how unique identifiers enable tracking along the care continuum and introduces indicators on test volume and positivity and on individuals testing positive.

Highlights early diagnosis as key to treatment success and reduced transmission, recommending monitoring of CD4 count and disease stage at diagnosis to detect late presenters. It stresses self-testing and community and network-based testing with timely linkage, supported by interoperable data systems and community-led monitoring.

Explains that prompt linkage to treatment improves viral suppression and reduces resistance, illness, death and transmission, and that it includes re-engaging people who have dropped out of care. It describes the core linkage indicator measuring the share of newly diagnosed people who start ART, disaggregated by time since diagnosis. It also covers partner and contact testing services with consent and confidentiality, their cascade data, and a survey-based indicator on key populations who know their status.
Notes that the annexes include examples of standardized HIV testing data collection tools from Malawi, such as testing, screening, confirmatory and self-test distribution registers.
Lists the minimum HIV testing data to record consistently across facility and community sites: test date, result, date of diagnosis, date the result was received and linkage to care where feasible.

A box summarizing new WHO HIV treatment recommendations relevant to patient monitoring, such as rapid and same-day ART initiation, updated first-, second- and third-line regimens and a revised viral load monitoring algorithm. It notes that patient tools, electronic records and the minimum dataset must be updated accordingly, including for revised antiretroviral toxicity indicators covering weight gain, cardiometabolic effects and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Explains that under WHO's treat-all policy, people on ART must be monitored over time as they move between facilities, with priority treatment indicators tracking the cascade from initiation or re-entry to retention, viral suppression, discontinuation, toxicity, loss to follow-up and death. It presents a table of these indicators, starting with ART coverage towards the second 95 target and total attrition. It describes updates to the attrition indicator and invites country feedback on its feasibility.

Stresses person-centred ART initiation and introduces the indicators on new ART patients and late initiation, with a table of WHO recommendations on when to start ART, including rapid and same-day initiation and exceptions. It covers monitoring of clinical management and lists paediatric monitoring priorities such as early infant diagnosis coverage and age at diagnosis and treatment start. It also notes the need for fine age disaggregation of testing and treatment indicators.

Describes updates to viral load monitoring, with the first test reviewed by six months after starting ART and a repeat test three months after an unsuppressed result following enhanced adherence counselling. It distinguishes treatment failure above 1,000 copies/mL from lower detectable levels and presents WHO's 2021 viral load testing algorithm with actions for each result.

Explains that retention on ART is key to viral suppression and lower mortality, citing sub-Saharan African data showing nearly one fifth stopped ART and 15–20% died within five years. It describes monitoring attrition and the role of unique identifiers in tracking people between facilities and avoiding miscounting of silent transfers.

Calls for analysis of attrition data to find facilities needing support and the causes of poor retention, from waiting times to drug toxicity. It explains that people counted as lost to follow-up are often silent transfers, deaths or discontinuations, and describes data-driven tracing and re-engagement, criteria for tracing and an updated patient card recording prior ARV exposure and restarts. It also mentions monitoring ART initiation alongside treatment interruption as people return to care.

Defines advanced HIV disease as a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 in adults and adolescents, and all children under five living with HIV, noting these people need closer follow-up. It describes the package of screening, prophylaxis and rapid ART recommended for advanced disease and the data elements to monitor it. It also stresses resource planning and monitoring for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and adverse drug reactions.

Explains why monitoring ARV drug safety is increasingly important as treatment scales up and newer drugs are introduced, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women. It describes WHO's recommended combination of approaches, such as pregnancy safety surveillance and active and routine toxicity monitoring. A table lists data elements for monitoring weight gain and cardiometabolic toxicity, including risk factors and drug exposure.

Describes early warning indicators of HIV drug resistance, a set of quality-of-care measures used to identify clinics where service gaps could foster resistance. It reviews viral, drug, patient and programme factors linked to resistance and presents a table of the current indicators and targets. It also describes a WHO tool for collecting and reporting the indicators and urges countries to use routine patient monitoring rather than parallel systems.

Sets out general child health monitoring for children living with HIV, such as growth, development, immunization and infant feeding, noting WHO guidance that mothers on ART with suppressed viral loads can breastfeed up to two years. It lists additional paediatric indicators, including viral suppression by age, psychosocial support and optimized second-line regimens, and stresses continuity of records as children move into adolescent and adult care.

Summarizes what is new in monitoring vertical transmission of HIV, including stronger tracking of the PMTCT cascade across services and over the full exposure period and an emphasis on elimination. It describes the priority indicator on viral suppression at labour and delivery and recent WHO recommendations relevant to pregnant and breastfeeding women. It explains that these changes require updates to patient monitoring tools and indicators.

Outlines the conceptual framework for monitoring PMTCT across multiple services and over a long period, from primary prevention and reproductive health services to treating mothers and following exposed infants to final diagnosis.

Explains that data tools must follow mother–baby pairs between service points and facilities, relying on unique identifiers, integration of HIV information into maternal and child health cards or electronic systems. It recommends integrating PMTCT and paediatric HIV services and their monitoring with maternal, newborn and child health care.

Describes the updated vertical transmission indicators, which since 2020 emphasize results like maternal viral suppression and early diagnosis of infants, with seven designated national priority indicators tied to key points in the risk period. A figure maps maternal and child health service points to the patient monitoring tools used at each, such as registers and cards for antenatal care, delivery and postnatal care.

Stresses following mother–infant pairs from antenatal and delivery care to child health and ART services, using a mother–infant pair register and recording the mother's identifier on the infant's record. It lists the care HIV-exposed infants should receive and be monitored for, such as prophylaxis, timely nucleic acid testing, feeding practices and final outcome testing. It sets out the minimum dataset for exposed infants, highlighting updates since 2017.

Summarizes 2020 updates to TB–HIV patient monitoring, including revised indicators on TB preventive treatment and rapid molecular TB testing and new shorter preventive regimens. It recalls WHO's collaborative TB/HIV activities and lists recent recommendations relevant to recording and reporting, such as new screening tools and starting ART within two weeks of TB treatment.

Describes TB-related services for people living with HIV that are measured through the HIV patient monitoring system, such as ART, case-finding, preventive treatment and infection control. A box lists the TB–HIV indicators, including national core indicators on preventive treatment initiation and completion and priority indicators on diagnostic testing.

Explains how HIV among TB patients is monitored through standardized TB treatment cards, registers and quarterly reports, increasingly in electronic systems such as DHIS2. It notes the need to reconcile ART and TB registers for indicators on ART among TB patients and that other TB–HIV indicators come from TB programme records.

Calls for strong coordination, referral and communication between TB and HIV services, supported by electronic systems and co-located clinics, to ensure joint care and reconciled records. It tabulates TB–HIV data elements for HIV patient cards and registers. It also lists additional HIV data elements recommended for TB treatment cards, such as unique identifier, CD4 count, viral load and ARV regimen.
A heading fragment reading 'and care', from the section title on monitoring service delivery for HIV treatment and care.

Introduces WHO's 2021 service delivery recommendations for HIV treatment and care, aimed at improving access, simplifying care and supporting return to care. It notes that the section presents eight key recommendations supporting differentiated service delivery and its monitoring.

Defines differentiated service delivery as a person-centred approach that adapts HIV services to people's needs while using resources efficiently, built on four elements: what, where, who and when. It describes four categories of differentiated ART models, from health worker-managed groups to individual facility and community models. It summarizes WHO recommendations on less frequent visits and refills, community delivery and task sharing with nurses, community health workers and lay providers.

Explains that patient monitoring systems and tools must be adapted to capture data from differentiated service delivery models, with updated patient cards, registers and reports. It stresses that the linked facility keeps clinical responsibility and that community site data should be entered promptly into facility systems to avoid parallel reporting and support tracking of missed pick-ups.

Notes that the key indicators for differentiated service delivery cover coverage, uptake and clinical outcomes, but that programme management also needs measures of client and worker experience, costs, efficiency and workload. It points to forthcoming WHO guidance and an existing ICAP framework for monitoring and evaluation.

Presents multi-month ARV dispensing (indicator DSD.1) as the minimum indicator when rolling out differentiated service delivery (DSD) for HIV treatment, noting it is also a Global AIDS Monitoring indicator. It suggests aligning drug pick-ups, clinical visits and dispensing for co-infections, and Table 3.8 defines five priority DSD indicators, including enrolment, retention and viral suppression in DSD models. Programmes are also advised to monitor whether eligibility criteria for DSD are applied correctly.

Explains how retention and viral suppression among people in DSD treatment models can be compared before and after implementation and assessed through adapted cohort reports. It stresses including DSD clients in cohort monitoring without double counting, and notes how treatment interruption is defined for people on longer dispensing intervals.

Suggests additional evaluation of DSD models, such as patient and provider satisfaction and cost-effectiveness, with indicators disaggregated by age, gender and key population. It describes tracing people who interrupt treatment, incorporating ART pick-up dates into tools to detect missed visits, and lists data to record on tracing outcomes and reasons.

Describes how DSD elements should be built into patient cards, registers and electronic records, including ART initiation outside facilities, DSD model enrolment and community and psychosocial interventions. It highlights monitoring CD4 at presentation and on return to care to identify advanced disease, and lists key data elements for DSD clients, such as pick-up dates and reasons for exclusion from DSD.

Sets out monitoring considerations for community-delivered ART, including developing community tools while keeping patient records at facilities, and protecting data confidentiality and security in community settings. It lists existing community ART and adherence club tools that countries can adapt. A Mozambique case study describes how its patient monitoring system, tools and DSD indicators were strengthened.

States WHO recommendations for monitoring key populations: data protection frameworks, no key population or criminalized-behaviour information in ART registers or reports, and clinically useful information only in secure patient records.

Explains why collecting identifiable data on stigmatized or criminalized behaviours from people on ART can harm clients and providers, through law enforcement use, underreporting and discrimination. It notes that behaviours change over time, so labelling someone as a key population member may not stay meaningful.

Advises that only clinically relevant information, such as drug dependence, opioid agonist therapy, hormone therapy or sexual risk, be recorded in identifiable clinical records for people on HIV treatment. Partner-related prevention interventions can be noted on the back of the patient card.

Explains that ART registers are not suitable for recording key population status, and that ART coverage among key populations should instead be measured through bio-behavioural and other surveys or de-identified case surveillance. It describes how key population programmes can confirm linkage to treatment while protecting identities, with an example from the EpiC programme in Malawi using triplicate referral tickets.

Defines trans and gender diverse people and advises recording both gender identity and sex assigned at birth on clinical records, or only male and female where being trans is highly stigmatized or penalized.

Introduces the minimum dataset for HIV patient monitoring, a standardized set of demographic, clinical and laboratory data elements with defined coding, and highlights new elements in the 2022 version. It then sets out key definitions along the care cascade, such as enrolment in HIV care, ART start, transfers, loss to follow-up and treatment outcomes. It notes WHO's recommendation of rapid ART initiation within seven days of diagnosis.

Gives WHO recommendations on standardized tools: a patient card or electronic record for every person diagnosed with HIV, ART registers wherever ART is provided, and simple standardized reporting by community ART providers. It describes the transfer and referral form and an overview figure of monitoring tools across HIV, maternal and child health and TB settings.

Describes how the facility-based HIV patient monitoring system follows people from diagnosis through ART to viral suppression and should produce actionable reports. It explains the steps for starting a patient card at any entry point and in integrated settings, and lists updates to the patient card, such as TB diagnostic tests, preventive therapy codes and immunizations.
Describes the HIV transfer and referral form, which carries key patient information between facilities and community ART sites and includes a counter-referral slip confirming successful transfer.

States WHO's recommendation that everyone starting ART be entered in a longitudinal ART register organized by start cohort and used to compile cohort and cross-sectional reports. It explains benefits for integrated settings and lists updates to the register, such as DSD enrolment, weight gain as a toxicity and fluconazole prophylaxis.

Explains the two reports built from the ART register: a cross-sectional report of current and cumulative patients, and a cohort report of outcomes at set intervals after starting ART. It describes how indicators such as new ART patients, late initiation and people on ART are drawn from these reports. It lists updates, including viral load timing and outcomes for people in DSD models.
Lists other recommended monitoring tools: appointment books to track missed visits and pharmacy data elements for monitoring adherence.

Describes the role of community ART providers under WHO's 2021 DSD recommendations, including task shifting, linking clients to facilities and distributing medicines in communities. It introduces a community-based ART monitoring tool and notes links to maternal, child health and TB services.
A section heading fragment on improving the quality and use of individual-level data for HIV patient monitoring.

Stresses the importance of good-quality individual-level data for patient management and progress towards the 95–95–95 targets, with data quality work institutionalized rather than ad hoc. It sets out data quality dimensions, confidentiality principles and a systems approach to data quality improvement. It describes practical checks, such as reconciling high viral load results between laboratory systems and facility registers. It ends with district-level triangulation of data sources to improve model inputs and subnational estimates.

Argues that data quality improvement matters only if data are used to improve services, and illustrates data use at patient, facility, district and national levels. It describes standardized information products, training, mentorship and supportive supervision, and making reports actionable with clear responsibilities. It also covers analysing loss-to-follow-up data to support tracing and lists data-use tasks for different facility staff.
A section heading fragment on adapting and implementing the HIV patient monitoring system.
Introduces guidance on adapting and implementing the HIV patient monitoring system, from coordination across programmes to transitioning between versions, on paper or electronic platforms.

Explains that the generic HIV patient monitoring system supports both integrated services and linked separate sites, and lists special considerations such as the service delivery model. Table 3.11 sets out 16 adaptation steps, from forming a technical working group and inventorying tools to defining indicators, training, coordinating partners and ensuring sustainable funding. A box describes the collaboration needed across HIV and other programmes, including standard minimum datasets and unique identifiers.

Describes staffing for HIV patient monitoring in WHO's HIV strategic information guidelines, with a table assigning roles from district teams to clinicians, data clerks and lay providers, and notes that task-shifting can extend capacity. It sets out recommendations for training, clinical mentoring and supportive supervision, including what mentoring visits should cover.

Explains why many high-burden countries are moving from paper to electronic HIV patient records, such as difficulty retrieving data and the need for linkage across services, while noting that coverage is incomplete. The block also includes the end of a box on supportive supervision using checklists.
The reference list for chapter 3 of the HIV strategic information guidelines, citing mainly WHO HIV, testing and TB guidance and modelling and data-use studies.
The opening page and contents of chapter 4, on integrating sexually transmitted infections, viral hepatitis and cervical cancer into HIV surveillance systems.

Lists five new key recommendations for chapter 4: person-centred HIV systems should monitor related infections, STI testing and treatment and recent STI history should be recorded, hepatitis B and C services should be measured for people with HIV and key populations, and cervical cancer screening should be recorded for women living with HIV.

Explains that STIs and viral hepatitis share transmission routes and risk profiles with HIV and are often served through linked services, so person-centred data systems can support their monitoring and universal health coverage. It introduces a minimum dataset and indicators for STIs, hepatitis and cervical cancer, linked by unique identifiers.

Describes the burden of STIs, with over a million curable infections a day, and the groups most vulnerable to them, with a figure of estimated 2020 cases of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis by sex. It links STIs to HIV acquisition and to the global health sector strategy for 2022–2030 and lists relevant WHO STI guidelines.

Presents a recommended minimum dataset for monitoring STIs in HIV programmes, covering visit dates, syndromic or laboratory diagnoses, tests and samples, confirmatory results and treatment prescribed and dispensed, noting the need for clear case definitions where treatment is symptom-based.

A table of priority STI indicators for HIV programmes, such as syphilis testing coverage, positivity and treatment coverage and treatment of symptomatic STIs, with numerators, denominators and notes on disaggregation and country-specific treatment rules.

Describes the global burden of hepatitis B and C, with 296 million and 58 million people infected in 2019 and over a million deaths a year, concentrated in certain countries and populations such as people who inject drugs. It explains shared prevention approaches with HIV, elimination strategies and the need for person-centred monitoring of the hepatitis care and cure cascade.

Presents a minimum dataset for viral hepatitis in HIV programmes, covering HBV and HCV test dates and results, treatment start and regimen and HCV cure testing, stressing disaggregation by HIV status.

A table of priority viral hepatitis indicators for HIV programmes, including HBV and HCV testing coverage, positivity, treatment and cure, aligned with WHO's hepatitis monitoring framework and global reporting systems.

Explains that cervical cancer risk is six times higher in women living with HIV, with faster progression and more recurrence, and that the HIV-attributable fraction exceeds 40% in parts of southern Africa. It calls for integrated services and restates WHO's screening strategy for women living with HIV from age 25 every 3 to 5 years.

A minimum dataset for cervical cancer screening and treatment among women living with HIV, covering HPV vaccination, primary and triage testing, pre-cancer treatment and follow-up, invasive cancer treatment and death. It notes that screening should also be offered to transgender men and other people with a cervix.

Presents four priority indicators for cervical cancer screening and treatment among women living with HIV, aligned with WHO screening guidance and the elimination strategy, with age disaggregation from 20 and inclusive, confidential gender categories.
The reference list for chapter 4, citing mainly studies and WHO strategies on STIs, viral hepatitis, HPV and cervical cancer in people living with HIV.
The opening page and contents of chapter 5, on using routine data for HIV surveillance, including methods for estimating incidence and prevalence, a minimum dataset and data quality needs.

Lists five new key recommendations for chapter 5: individual-level HIV surveillance linking data over time, a minimum routine clinical dataset to support incidence measurement, CD4 testing at diagnosis, reporting mortality and causes of death, and stronger electronic case surveillance.

Explains why tracking HIV incidence, prevalence and mortality matters for guiding the response and meeting global targets, and how routine person-centred data can complement other sources. It describes common measurement methods, including population-based and bio-behavioural surveys, cohort studies and mathematical models such as Spectrum, with their strengths and limits. It also addresses mortality measurement. It ends by advising against routinely collecting key population information where safety is a concern and suggesting triangulation of programme and survey data.

Describes how countries combine individual patient-level and aggregated data, noting that manual aggregation limits flexible analysis and quality checks. It outlines what HIV case surveillance should capture and the rights-based framework, case definitions and data systems it requires.

Introduces methods for estimating HIV incidence and prevalence from routinely collected individual-level programme data to inform models such as Spectrum, including seroconversion rates as a proxy for incidence.

Lists seven methods for using routine data to estimate HIV incidence and explains the first, CD4/AIDS back-calculation, which infers time since infection from CD4 levels at diagnosis. It describes how missing CD4 values can be imputed and why the method is often the only option in concentrated epidemics. A Brazilian example shows the approach applied to national surveillance data, with a map of new HIV cases by municipality in 2019.

Explains how HIV retesting supports prevention and re-linkage to care, the factors linked to retesting, and why some people who already know they are positive retest. It discusses how longitudinal testing data can identify duplicate diagnoses and support a cyclical care cascade. It describes using seroconversions in routine testing data to estimate incidence, the biases involved, and a study where behavioural and serological estimates agreed closely.

Explains how recency assays can estimate incidence in population surveys, but in routine programmes are best applied to groups tested for reasons unrelated to risk, such as antenatal clients, and not used for individual clinical management. It discusses biases from non-random testing and how testing history, viral load and ART exposure improve classification of recent infections. It concludes that recency data on distribution and trends should be compared with other surveillance methods for estimating incidence.

Describes the long use of pregnant women at antenatal clinics as a sentinel population for HIV trends and the shift to near-universal routine antenatal testing. It discusses how changes in testing or reporting practices can distort trends and why antenatal prevalence differs systematically from that of the general population. It lists conditions for routine antenatal data to be reliable for surveillance, such as high attendance and testing coverage and using only the first test per pregnancy. It also considers incidence during pregnancy and the postpartum period.

Notes that methods estimating HIV incidence from age-specific prevalence rely on strong assumptions and are no longer recommended, though they may still indicate plausible limits. It explains the assumptions involved and includes a figure of people living with HIV by timing of infection.

Describes how phylogenetic analysis of HIV sequences, for instance from drug resistance surveillance, can reveal transmission clusters and recent rapid transmission, as used in the US Ending the Epidemic programme. It notes limited feasibility in resource-limited settings and illustrates how a cluster grows between samples taken two years apart.

Sets out the advantages of using routine data in modelling HIV incidence and prevalence, such as low cost and easy updating, and the difficulties in key population epidemics. It stresses engaging key population organizations and describes data cleaning and imputation methods for missing values, favouring multiple imputation.

Explains that national surveillance systems need a standardized minimum set of reportable data elements, such as diagnosis date, CD4 count and viral load, to estimate incidence and prevalence. It recommends linking case reports to laboratory data and collecting CD4 at diagnosis as a minimum. Table 5.1 lists the required elements, with notes on recency testing and use of electronic records.

Notes that routine data quality depends on how well information is captured and cleaned, and that inconsistent reporting can be mistaken for real changes in coverage. It calls for a culture of data quality assessment and use so that routine facility data can sustainably monitor incidence, prevalence and the HIV response.

The reference list for the chapter on routine data for HIV surveillance, citing WHO and UNAIDS guidance, population surveys, and studies on back-calculation, recency testing, antenatal surveillance, phylogenetics and modelling tools.
The contents listing for Chapter 6 on digital health data, covering interoperability, unique identifiers, and privacy, security and data access.

Sets out updated and new recommendations on digital health data: building interoperability standards and transparent data governance, publishing data-use rules, and using anonymous unique identifiers to link a person's records across services. It also covers privacy, security and restricting access to personal data to authorized parties.

Introduces the shift from paper to digital health data, describing its opportunities for better outcomes and its risks for privacy and individual rights, especially in HIV. It stresses that governance and a protective policy environment matter as much as technology, and notes that some aspects of care are hard to capture digitally. It discusses the digital divide that limits access to digital services. A case example from Malawi describes a digital platform for managing HIV programme performance that flags facilities with worrying trends.

Defines interoperability as the ability of systems to access, exchange and use data across organizations and boundaries, and outlines organizational, legal and technical types. It describes benefits at the point of care, within and between facilities, such as reducing loss to follow-up and improving supply decisions, and the value of publishing standards and business processes. It notes that full interoperability is hard to achieve and needs incentives at technical and legal levels.

Explains organizational interoperability as aligning the goals and relationships of organizations so data can be exchanged, and describes supporting measures such as national strategy documents. It illustrates business process mapping with an example workflow for HIV testing.

Explains legal interoperability, which removes legal barriers to data sharing and sets rules on ownership, protection, privacy, individual access and storage. It continues the HIV testing business process diagram.

Explains technical interoperability, covering semantic and syntactic standards and secure exchange protocols developed by bodies such as ISO, HL7 and SNOMED International. It uses everyday product standards as an analogy and names JSON and XML as common data formats.

Explains the need to share health data between facilities and systems and describes the HL7 FHIR specification, its resources, formats and exchange protocols and why it is popular. Box 6.5 uses WHO's digital documentation of COVID-19 certificates to illustrate technical, semantic and governance aspects of interoperability.

Describes unique identifiers (UIDs) that let people be recognised across HIV and other health services, stressing that they should be content-free and hold no personal details such as birth date or location. It outlines their benefits for linking records and efficiency, and the security and confidentiality risks they pose. The section closes by stating that sensitive details such as sexual orientation should not be collected unless clinically relevant, and that relevant clinical information can be kept in secure records.

Recommends a step-wise path for introducing health UIDs, moving from situation analysis through data security and data use to programme improvement and sustainability. It details what the situation analysis should cover, including existing identifiers, data systems and capacities, and privacy and security laws and policies. It also covers costing benefits, maturity stages for technical components and integrating HIV monitoring into a national UID system. The section ends by stressing planning for policies, maintenance, hardware, software, staff and analytical capacity.

Outlines the system architecture for a UID system, pointing to ASTM, ISO and CEN technical standards for health identifiers. It describes three facility layers (paper only, reliable power, and network) and the equipment each needs, from data-entry workstations to central, regional or cloud registry servers, noting data-protection questions when data are stored abroad. It then covers interoperability and the technical components and attributes of a UID, ending with how registration and service data are captured and linked to commodity inventory systems.

Warns that growing volumes of centralised digital health data raise the risk and impact of breaches, so systems must be designed for privacy, security and confidentiality from the outset. An example describes a real-time, person-centred electronic system for services to people who use drugs, with safeguards such as access levels, encryption and de-identified dashboards. Table 6.4 then sets out five types of health data, from personally identifiable to non-personal information.

Recommends a situation analysis as the first step in securing a digital health system, using the UNAIDS privacy, confidentiality and security assessment tool run through stakeholder workshops. Table 6.5 lists sample questions on governance and policy and related areas at facility, data warehouse and policy levels.

Argues that patients should have legally protected access to and control over their own health data and recommends rights-based legal protections. The continuation of Table 6.5 lists questions on access control, data release, transmission security and disposal. It then lists key legal provisions for personal health data, such as portability, revoking access, data protection officers, breach notification and penalties, and cites the EU GDPR principle of data minimisation.

Notes that legal protection of people's access to their health data brings indirect benefits, such as encouraging interoperability standards, content-free identifiers and digital platforms to hold personal records.
The reference list for the chapter on digital health data, citing WHO digital health guidance, digital adaptation kits, COVID-19 certificate specifications, technical standards and GDPR articles.

The opening page of Chapter 7 on strengthening data use from all sources, listing its sections, including quality of care, community-led monitoring, logistics systems, surveys, modelling and data quality review.

Argues that a national HIV monitoring and evaluation framework should combine multiple data sources, each with strengths and limits, and map data elements to users and purposes. It lists the many ways HIV and related data can be collected and stresses simple recording and reporting. The section ends with points on community data, such as linking identifiers to avoid double counting between community and facility services.

Lists the most common sources of HIV programme data, from routine health information and case surveillance to laboratory and logistics systems, vital statistics, population surveys, special studies and community-led monitoring. It also outlines what the rest of the chapter covers.
A fragment of a section heading on measuring and improving the quality of person-centred care.

Sets out the rationale for measuring quality of care, citing estimates that poor-quality care causes millions of deaths and huge economic losses in low- and middle-income countries. It argues that people receiving HIV services need high-quality care, that quality must be measured across health system levels, and that WHO quality definitions should be used locally.

Describes how quality of HIV care should be measured mainly through existing information systems and routine data, with a framework that defines data sources, capacity, triangulation and use for improvement. It stresses capturing integrated, longitudinal care across service points, considering the diversity of clients and keeping data anonymised. The section also notes related services, such as palliative and psychosocial care, that should be considered when measuring quality.

Highlights the role of communities and community-led organisations in defining and measuring quality of HIV care and holding stakeholders accountable, pointing to community-led monitoring as a complement to routine data.

Describes what a quality-of-care measurement framework should include, such as what matters most to service users, multiple stakeholders, validated tools, and clinical and patient-reported indicators of experience, perception, knowledge and outcomes. It introduces a person-centred indicator framework (Table 7.2) for selecting indicators.

Presents Table 7.3, the priority indicators recommended for monitoring quality of HIV care across prevention, testing, treatment and other care stages, such as linkage to treatment, viral load suppression and coverage of differentiated service delivery models. It notes that more indicators are in a web annex and that most come from earlier chapters and the minimum dataset. It ends by urging that quality concepts be built into national strategic information frameworks and routine systems.

Describes community-led monitoring as an accountability and advocacy strategy led by organisations of people living with HIV and key populations to improve the quality and accessibility of services. It distinguishes it from community-based service delivery and stresses that communities should set its focus free from outside influence. The section explains how its findings, combined with routine person-centred data, can reveal gaps that might otherwise be missed.

Explains why an uninterrupted supply of antiretroviral drugs and diagnostics is essential to HIV programmes and what a good distribution system achieves. It notes that drug dispensing data can measure multi-month dispensing under differentiated service delivery. It argues that linking logistics management information systems with deduplicated, de-identified patient-level data helps avoid wastage and stock-outs, with quarterly review recommended.

Describes how health facility assessments monitor the availability and readiness of HIV services, including staff, equipment, medicines and diagnostics, and warns that private facilities are often under-represented in samples. It mentions tools such as the Service Availability and Readiness Assessment and includes part of a case study from Malawi on electronic medical records.

Describes how civil registration and vital statistics provide data on births, deaths and causes of death for HIV mortality, and the conditions for these data to be usable, such as confidentiality and completeness. It notes that verbal autopsy and other special studies, and linking data systems, can fill gaps.

Explains that population-based surveys capture people not reached by health services and complement routine data, listing survey types such as DHS, AIS, PHIA, bio-behavioural surveys and the Stigma Index. It sets out considerations for using survey indicators, including their cost, infrequency, limited geographic precision and the difficulty of surveying children and adolescents.

Explains why modelled estimates are needed for numbers of people living with HIV, new infections and AIDS deaths, and how models such as Spectrum AIM combine survey, surveillance and programme data. It notes that models allow comparison over time and across countries and can answer other policy questions, and recommends including model results in regular data reviews.

Describes the harmonized data quality review framework developed by WHO, the Global Fund and Gavi, recommended for integration into health information systems and at least annual national review. It lists the quality dimensions assessed, such as completeness, timeliness and internal and external consistency, and notes that subnational and facility managers may review data more often.

Stresses that HIV programmes need regular evaluation and operational research alongside routine data, with a prioritized evaluation agenda and studies managed as formal projects, noting that individual-level data are better suited to research questions.

The reference list for the chapter on HIV data sources, citing WHO guidance on surveys, quality of care and consolidated HIV guidelines, survey programmes such as DHS and AIS, and data collection tools.
The contents page of Chapter 8 on priority indicators, listing sections by programme area from HIV prevention and testing to hepatitis, cervical cancer and stigma.
Introduces Chapter 8, which details priority and core indicators organized under prevention, testing and treatment, related infections, impact, and stigma and discrimination.

Explains why data should be disaggregated by geography, age, gender, priority population and patient group to assess equity and close gaps for underserved groups. It discusses age bands and other disaggregation categories and the need for consistent categories across indicators. It ends by warning that fine-grained disaggregation in small areas can breach confidentiality where stigma or criminalization are common.

Explains that most priority indicators have no fixed reporting period and can be calculated over different periods, while some track individuals' service use over time, such as follow-up viral load testing, which may need longitudinal registers or digital systems.
Stresses that monitoring systems should capture community-based service data and avoid double counting people referred between community and facility services.

Sets out the priority indicators for HIV prevention, each with what it measures, rationale, numerator, denominator, measurement method and disaggregation. It opens with condoms distributed and people receiving pre-exposure prophylaxis, and covers the range of prevention services. It ends with indicators on condom use at last sex for the general population and key populations, with notes on survey sources and adapting recall periods to local context.

Sets out the priority indicators for HIV testing services, starting with the number and percentage of people living with HIV who know their status (the first 95). It explains how to estimate this from case surveillance or models and how to deduplicate records. Further indicators cover testing services and yield. It ends with a new indicator on HIV retesting coverage among key populations, measured through survey questions.

Sets out the priority indicators for HIV treatment, starting with the number and percentage of people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, linked to the second 95 target. It explains how to calculate the numerator accounting for attrition and which denominators to use. Further indicators cover treatment outcomes and vertical transmission. It ends with HIV prevalence among antenatal clinic attendees and the conditions under which these data can be used for surveillance.

Sets out the priority indicators for TB/HIV, starting with initiation of TB preventive treatment among eligible people on ART and a formula for calculating eligibility. Disaggregation by gender, age and regimen is specified. The indicators follow a screening cascade for high-burden settings. They end with the share of people newly started on ART and diagnosed with active TB who began TB treatment.

Sets out the priority indicators for differentiated service delivery, starting with a new indicator on multi-month dispensing of antiretroviral medicines and its rationale for adherence and system efficiency. It explains numerators by months of supply dispensed. It ends with viral load suppression among people enrolled in differentiated ART models, monitored where electronic systems exist.

Sets out the priority indicators for sexually transmitted infections, starting with a new indicator on syphilis testing coverage among people using HIV prevention services, people living with HIV and pregnant women. Each indicator gives rationale, numerator, denominator, measurement and disaggregation. Further indicators cover STI diagnosis and treatment. The section ends with repeat diagnoses of the same STI syndrome, which may signal inadequate treatment or an untreated partner.

Defines new viral hepatitis indicators for HIV strategic information, starting with hepatitis B surface antigen testing coverage among people using HIV prevention services, people living with HIV and pregnant women. For each indicator it sets out what is measured, the rationale, numerator, denominator, measurement method and disaggregation. Further indicators cover hepatitis B and C treatment and outcomes, such as people with HIV cured of hepatitis C, with disaggregation by medicine type and region. Footnotes clarify gender categories and data confidentiality considerations for key populations.

Defines new cervical cancer indicators for women living with HIV, including the number screened with any test, with guidance on counting each woman once and using facility registers. Further indicators address follow-up and treatment of screen-positive women and survival 12 months after a cervical cancer diagnosis, disaggregated by age, stage and area. The section ends by introducing a cervical cancer survival indicator.

Defines the HIV incidence indicator as new infections per 1000 uninfected people, with its rationale, measurement through programme data or modelling tools such as Spectrum, and disaggregation by gender, age and route of transmission.

Defines the AIDS mortality indicator as AIDS-related deaths per 100,000 population, explaining its purpose, data sources such as vital registration or modelling, and disaggregation by gender, age and key population.

Defines indicators on avoidance of health care because of stigma and discrimination among key populations and among people living with HIV, using survey questions about avoiding testing, care or treatment. It gives numerator, denominator, data sources such as the Stigma Index, and disaggregation, and ends with WHO contact details and the ISBN.

The front matter of WHO's 2022 consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information, with ISBNs and Creative Commons licence terms. It also contains a detailed table of contents running through chapters on prevention, testing, treatment, data systems and priority indicators.
